scope: All visitor-facing source-derived language, including repeated figures and takeaways.
countingMethod: Each factual paraphrase and repetition is charged to every source needed for the claim. Technical explanations and the verified Library connection are identified separately.

fragments.text: Microsoft reportedly plans to more than triple its data-centre capacity by 2032.
Reuters reported on September 10 that Microsoft plans to expand its data-centre capacity from about 12 gigawatts now to about 38 gigawatts by 2032.
Reuters reported on September 10 that Microsoft plans to expand its data-centre capacity from about 12 gigawatts now to about 38 gigawatts by 2032.
fragments.rationale: The compound date-and-roadmap sentence uses Reuters for September 10 and both reports for 12-to-38.

fragments.text: Reuters was summarizing Bloomberg reporting based on people familiar with the plans. Microsoft did not immediately respond to Reuters.

About 2 gigawatts of the current capacity is centred on AI-specific chips. The report says about one-third of the planned 38 gigawatts would be AI-specific. The roadmap therefore covers AI and other cloud computing.
Data centres are physical buildings filled with servers. They host the machinery that runs AI services and other cloud work.
fragments.rationale: Verified Library chapter 17.1 defines the physical data-centre role.

fragments.text: A gigawatt measures power: the rate at which electricity can be supplied or used at a moment. In this report, 38 gigawatts describes the capacity Microsoft plans to have online in 2032. It is not a reading of electricity Microsoft is consuming today, and it does not tell us how much energy those facilities would use over a day or year.
fragments.rationale: Technical unit explanation required to distinguish power capacity from energy consumption; the 38-GW repetition is charged separately below.

fragments.text: In this report, 38 gigawatts describes the capacity Microsoft plans to have online in 2032.
Bloomberg’s public excerpt says the roadmap counts facilities Microsoft owns or leases. It leaves out computing rented from outside providers such as CoreWeave.
The reported expansion would build more of the physical infrastructure behind AI and other online services. It says Microsoft is planning room for much more computing.
It does not show how fully those facilities will run or how much electricity they will consume over time.
Microsoft is reportedly planning data centres with about 38 gigawatts of capacity by 2032, up from about 12 now.
Microsoft is reportedly planning data centres with about 38 gigawatts of capacity by 2032, up from about 12 now.
Capacity is how much power the infrastructure can support at a moment—not how much energy Microsoft is already using.

AI Fundamentals 101: Data Centres and Energy — What’s Actually Inside explains that data centres are physical buildings filled with servers. It is the useful starting point for understanding what this reported capacity plan would build.
fragments.rationale: Verified AI Fundamentals chapter 17.1 destination and physical data-centre explanation.
